PlacementPredict — Machine Learning System Report

Predicting student placement outcomes · supervised classification · data → model → serve → monitor
Generated 06 October 2026 · M1 system · M2 linear · M3 trees · M4 unsupervised

1. Executive summary

PlacementPredict answers one question: will this student be placed? A profile of ~30 inputs passes through a frozen pre-processing pipeline, is scored by a trained classifier, and returns an outcome plus a probability in milliseconds. This report walks the complete machine-learning lifecycle in plain language — suitable for anyone to read, no ML background required.

50,000Student records

66%Placement rate
Logistic RegressionDeployed model (best F1)

2. PlacementPredict as a system (M1)

Every ML product follows the same lifecycle; each stage has a concrete home in this codebase:

Raw data→ Clean→ Features→ Train set→ Model→ Artefact→ Serve→ Monitor→ Retrain
Lifecycle stageWhere it lives in code
Raw datadata/placement_data.csv — 50,000 student profiles
Cleaning & feature engineeringsrc/preprocessing.py — impute, standardise, encode
Training setdata/preprocessed_train.csv — stratified 80/20 split
Training scriptsrc/models.py — four classifiers + metrics
Model registrymodels/*.pkl, models/default_model.pkl
Serving frameworkapp/app.py, src/serving.py — form + JSON API
Monitoring/api/health — artefact state, model, metrics
Retraining loopscripts/pipeline.py — one command rebuilds everything
What kind of learning? Supervised classification — labels exist (Placed / Not Placed) and the model learns profile → outcome. It is not unsupervised (no label discovery) and not reinforcement learning (no agent, no reward). Clustering in M4 only explores the same data.
One prediction, end to end: HTTP POST → feature lookup → pipeline.transform() → predict_proba() → JSON. Batch prediction runs the identical path over many rows — one code path, so single and batch scoring can never disagree.
The training–serving boundary. The bug that breaks the most production systems is training-serving skew — features computed differently at serve time than at train time. Feature stores keep one canonical definition; here the fitted pipeline.pkl is exactly that: fit once on training data, reused verbatim everywhere.
Course scope: classical ML and ML engineering live here (M1–M4). Deep learning moves to DLAC, generative models to GALE, LLMs to NLPL.

3. Data & exploratory analysis (M1)

The dataset holds 50,000 students and 32 attributes. 19,976 cells are missing (five skill columns) and are repaired in preprocessing. The target is imbalanced about 2:1 toward placed students — which is why F1 and AUC, not accuracy alone, decide the winner.

Insight: CGPA, aptitude and coding scores cleanly separate placed from not-placed students; semester grades correlate strongly with CGPA, so the model relies on a compact set of academic signals.

4. Data preparation pipeline (M1)

1 · CleanDrop ID, IsAnomaly and Salary Package (label leakage).
2 · ImputeMedian for numerics, most-frequent for categories.
3 · ScaleStandardScaler so gradient descent converges.
4 · EncodeOne-hot for categories, ordinal for the two tiers.
5 · SplitStratified 80/20, random_state = 42.
6 · FreezeFitted transformer pickled as pipeline.pkl.

5. Linear models (M2)

Regularisation: ridge (L2) shrinks weights smoothly, lasso (L1) drives weak weights to exactly zero, elastic net combines both. The geometry explains the sparsity — the loss contour meets the L1 diamond at a corner, and a corner means a zero weight.

Why L1 produces sparsity

Sigmoid & cross-entropy loss

Logistic regression computes P(placed) = σ(w·x + b): a hyperplane boundary plus a sigmoid, trained by gradient descent on cross-entropy with ridge regularisation. Coefficients are log-odds, so every score can be explained to a stakeholder. Feature scaling matters for gradient descent — not for the trees in M3. Multinomial (softmax) regression generalises the same idea to k classes; this task is binary.

Categorical features & missing values: one-hot for unordered categories, ordinal for ordered ones (target and embedding encodings are advanced alternatives); deletion, mean/median, model-based imputation and missingness flags were compared — median / most-frequent is what production uses here.

6. Tree-based models (M3)

Decision trees split greedily on Gini impurity and stop at depth/leaf limits; cost-complexity pruning trims branches whose removal barely changes the error. A single deep tree overfits — the classic bias–variance curve below.

Random forests bag bootstrap samples with feature subsampling to cut variance and give an out-of-bag error for free. Boosting fits each new tree to the residual gradient of the loss; histogram-based learners with leaf-wise growth (XGBoost / LightGBM — and sklearn's HistGradientBoosting used here) are the modern industrial workhorses on tabular data. Feature importance comes in three flavours: Gini importance, permutation importance, and SHAP values (preview level).

Why trees win on tabular data: no scaling, native handling of missing values and mixed types, cheap tuning, non-linear interactions for free. Neural networks win on images, text and audio — DLAC / NLPL territory.

ROC curves

Confusion matrix — Logistic Regression

Reading the table: accuracy is the share of correct calls; precision is how reliable a “placed” call is; recall is how many truly placed students we catch; F1 balances both; AUC measures ranking quality. All four models exceed 90% accuracy — Logistic Regression is deployed for the best F1 combined with interpretability.

8. Serving the prediction (M1)

POST /api/predict→ feature lookup→ pipeline.transform()→ predict_proba()→ JSON
  • /prediction — interactive form with a live result card;
  • /api/predict — JSON in / JSON out for other systems;
  • /api/health — artefact state and metrics for monitoring;
  • /report/export — this report as a self-contained HTML file.

The frozen pipeline means the transform at serve time is byte-for-byte the transform used in training — the practical defence against training–serving skew.

9. Unsupervised learning (M4)

No labels here — structure, segments and anomalies. K-means with the elbow method and silhouette score finds three coherent student segments; hierarchical clustering reads merge structure from a dendrogram; DBSCAN grows clusters by density and marks noise points as outliers; PCA compresses features (always standardise first); t-SNE and UMAP visualise high dimensions — but distances in their spaces are not meaningful. Isolation forest and one-class SVM detect anomalies without labels, with autoencoders covered in DLAC.

K-means elbow

Student segments (3-D)

DBSCAN clusters & outliers

PCA variance & dendrogram

Isolation forest anomalies

The production trick: fit k-means, append each student's segment id as one more feature, and let the supervised classifier use group membership as extra signal — unsupervised structure feeding a supervised model.

10. Conclusions, limitations & reproduction

  • Academic performance dominates placement outcomes; skills (aptitude, coding, interviews) add signal.
  • Predictions are a decision aid — they cannot capture company demand, interview luck or market swings.
  • The ~2:1 imbalance means accuracy alone would mislead; F1 and AUC are tracked instead.
  • Retraining on fresh cohorts each semester keeps the model honest as profiles drift.
Reproduce everything:
pip install -r requirements.txt
python scripts/pipeline.py — rebuilds training data, models, metrics and every chart.
python app/app.py — serves the web app at http://localhost:5000.
In the web app press Ctrl+S to save this report, or use the export button.
